title: Build: replicated KV store
summary: Leader/follower replication over HTTP between real processes: a checksummed WAL, pull replication, async vs semi-sync, lag measurement, lease-based failover with epochs as fencing tokens, divergent-log truncation and read-your-writes tokens, all tested by killing, partitioning and freezing processes.

units.title: A durable single node: the write-ahead log

labs.title: Write-ahead log: CRC-32C framed records, fsync before ack, torn-tail and corruption recovery, contiguous indexes, durable truncation

Replicated KV as real processes: node (leader/follower, pull replication, async/semi-sync, lag, read-your-writes) and coordinator (leases, failover, epochs, demotion), tested with SIGKILL, SIGSTOP, partitions and torn WALs

outcomes.text: Implement a write-ahead log with checksummed, length-prefixed records and explain exactly which crash states recovery must handle (torn tail, corrupt record, missing directory entry) and why an ack must come after fsync.
Build pull-based log shipping where the follower's fetch position is its acknowledgement, and explain why pull beats push for catch-up, backpressure and failure handling.

Choose between async and semi-sync replication for a requirement by stating the RPO, the write latency and the availability cost of each, and demonstrate the acknowledged-write loss of async on a real crash.
Measure replication lag in records and seconds from the leader's side, and explain why a follower's self-reported lag lies during a partition.
Design lease-based failure detection and failover: detection time, the wait for the old lease, choosing the most up-to-date follower, and the clock assumption leases depend on.
Use epochs as fencing tokens so that a returning or paused old leader can neither acknowledge writes nor corrupt followers, and implement epoch-based log matching that truncates a divergent suffix.
Provide read-your-writes on followers with a version token and a bounded wait-then-redirect, and explain what it does not give you (monotonic reads across replicas, linearizability).
Write a design rationale that predicts the outcome of each failure-injection scenario, then compare the predictions with what the tests and break-it runs observed.

Explain why a single sentinel is a single point of failure for failover and how a majority-based design (Raft, a Sentinel quorum, a consensus-backed lease) removes it, and estimate the cost of group commit and pipelined fetches.
